title: Sustainable wildlife harvests can mitigate land use change
content:
Abstract
Habitat loss to agricultural production is expected to increase globally more than 3 million square kilometers by 2050. Food from wildlife harvests is critical to the livelihoods of millions of people worldwide and when done sustainably, could help mitigate habitat loss in response to increasing food demands. Even in the United States, wildlife harvests through sustainable hunting can significantly contribute to the sustainable maintenance of landscapes. We quantified harvests of native ungulates and non-native feral pigs (Sus scrofa) in the United States during the 2024–2025 hunting season to estimate the amount of habitat potentially spared from land use change if an equivalent mass of domestic beef cattle were produced for consumption. We estimated that reported harvests exceeded 6.9 million native ungulates nationally, representing 1.07 million domestic livestock animal unit equivalents (AUEs). Including feral pigs (Sus scrofa) increased reported harvest to almost 10.8 million individuals and 1.39 million AUEs. Raising an equivalent number of cattle AUEs would require 5100–7600 km2 of land (6700–10,000 km2 including feral pigs). Though wild meat derived from these and other harvests will not eliminate land conversion for agricultural purposes, policies that enhance sustainable wildlife harvests of native ungulates and increase harvests and consumption of non-native species (e.g., feral pigs) can further mitigate habitat loss. These results demonstrate that mitigation of habitat loss through sustainable harvests of native wildlife along with harvests of non-native species are important conservation benefits of wildlife management.
